snippet.title: Oxygen Was 35 Percent When Giants Walked — Someone Cut the Trees and Shrunk Everything
snippet.description: Thirty-five percent. That's how much oxygen was in Earth's atmosphere three hundred million years ago. Today it's twenty-one. That difference produced dragonflies with seventy-centimeter wingspans, millipedes two and a half meters long, and vertebrates significantly larger than anything alive today. The official explanation for those sizes is the oxygen itself. What the official explanation doesn't close is what was producing that oxygen at levels the current biosphere cannot reproduce. Robert Berner of Yale spent thirty years building the most cited geochemical model of deep-time atmospheric oxygen. His GEOCARB model, published in Science, requires photosynthetic productivity parameters that significantly exceed what reconstructed Carboniferous forests of forty-five-meter lycopsids can produce. The gap is documented. The numbers don't close. Steven Pons published the same mismatch in Palaeogeography Palaeoclimatology Palaeoecology. Peter Ward and Joe Kirschvink addressed it in A New History of Life. The Carboniferous Rainforest Collapse ended the forest that was producing thirty-five percent. After it was gone, oxygen never returned to that level. The giants that lived in that atmosphere disappeared with it. The Smithsonian Annual Report of 1873 contains field descriptions of anomalous skeletal remains from American burial mounds. A complete public catalog of what the Smithsonian collected in the nineteenth century does not exist. This video follows the evidence. Not the theory. The evidence.

snippet.title: The Loggers Who Reached Northern California in 1850 Found Stumps Already Cut — No Tool Could Match
snippet.description: In 1850, the first logging crews reached the coast of Northern California. They came for the redwoods. The trees stood taller than anything a white man had seen on the continent, three hundred feet high, trunks twenty feet across, bark thick as a man's forearm. No roads in the forest. No saw had touched it before that day. That is the official history. But when the crews began felling timber and clearing ground, they found stumps. Enormous stumps. Wider than any standing tree around them. The cut faces were flat. Horizontal. Not wind breakage, because wind snaps wood at angles and leaves ragged splintered edges. Not lightning, because lightning scores a vertical groove and splits the trunk from crown to root. These were level cuts. On several stumps the surface of the cut still held parallel grooves running in one direction, the signature of a blade drawn repeatedly across the grain. Saw marks. The loggers knew what saw work looked like because they did it every day of their working lives. And what they saw on those stumps was saw work.

One of the richest cities on Earth, capital of a global empire stretching from Brazil to India, from Africa to the Far East. Gold flows from the mines of Minas Gerais, spices arrive from Asia, and faith governs every street, square, and soul.

This film reconstructs Lisbon at the peak of its power—five years before the earthquake of 1755 erased much of the old city forever. Through historically grounded AI reconstruction, we walk its markets, convents, palaces, taverns, and narrow streets. We witness devotion and cruelty, wealth and hunger, splendor and fear coexisting within the same walls.

From the Alfama’s ancient Moorish alleys to the commercial heart of the Baixa, from the shadow of the Inquisition to the quiet routines of monks and laborers, this is Lisbon as its people knew it—alive, confident, and unaware of the catastrophe to come.

This is not legend.
This is not nostalgia.
This is a city reconstructed just before it vanished.

snippet.description:
The Night Galveston Was Erased explores the terrifying true story of America's deadliest storm and the 1900 hurricane that changed history forever. Discover how the wealthiest city in Texas was destroyed in a single night by the most fatal natural disaster in US history.

In this historical documentary, we deep dive into the Galveston Hurricane of 1900, an event so catastrophic it remains the deadliest weather event the United States has ever faced. snippet.title: How the Book of Kells was saved from Vikings
snippet.description:
Ever wondered why ancient Irish round towers have doors 3 meters off the ground? It wasn’t just for structure—it was for survival. In the 9th century, monks fleeing Viking attacks in Scotland brought the legendary Book of Kells to Kells, Ireland. To protect this priceless manuscript, they hid it—and themselves—inside these towers, pulling the ladder up behind them. Learn the hidden history behind Ireland’s round towers and one of the world’s most beautiful books.

snippet.title: New England's Stone Chambers Were Sealed Before the Puritans Arrived — They Were Locked From Inside
snippet.description: Across New England, from Maine to Connecticut, from Vermont to Putnam County, New York, there are stone chambers buried in the earth. Over two hundred in Putnam County alone. Dozens in Vermont. Dozens more in Massachusetts and New Hampshire. They are built into hillsides, sunk beneath forest floors, hidden under centuries of soil and roots. The walls are unmortared stone, laid using corbelling, where each course overhangs the one below until the walls curve inward and meet beneath a capstone slab weighing one to several tons. This is not farmhouse construction. This is Bronze Age engineering, the same method used for Mycenaean tholos tombs in Greece. Inside there are shelves, niches, ventilation holes. Entrances of nearly every chamber face the same direction. Some align with the winter solstice. In 1977, Vermont's Division for Historic Preservation concluded the chambers were not burial vaults, not kilns, not furnaces.

snippet.title: The Entire History of Iran in 21 Minutes (Full Documentary)
snippet.description:
5,000 Years. One Unbroken Identity. This is the Entire History of Iran.

From the rise of the first global superpower to the modern-day brink of extinction, the story of the Iranian plateau is the ultimate saga of human resilience. In just 21 minutes, we use AI Reconstruction to bring ancient Persia to life, exploring how this civilization survived the world's most brutal conquerors—from Alexander the Great to the Mongol Hordes.

In this full documentary, we dive deep into the Achaemenid Empire, the architectural wonders of Persepolis, and the legendary leadership of Cyrus the Great. We trace the evolution of Persian culture through the Islamic Golden Age, the Safavid Renaissance, and the turbulent Pahlavi era, leading directly into the high-stakes geopolitics of 2026.

Why has Iran remained a dominant force for five millennia? How does its ancient past shape its current defiance against global superpowers today? Witness the 5,000-year resistance of a nation that refuses to be erased.

snippet.title: Lisbon 1755 ( AI Reconstruction )
snippet.description:
Step back in time to Lisbon on the morning of November 1st, 1755 with an AI-generated reconstruction, inspired by the detailed azulejo panoramas and engravings of Gabriel del Barco, Georg Braun, Franz Hogenberg, and other period artists who documented Portugal's golden age between 1598–1730. 

All historical details are interpreted using AI for cinematic visualisation but much effort has been made to maintain accuracy to the source images and to the colours, materials and composition as it would have been at the time.

The most important source is Gabriel del Barco's monumental 23-meter azulejo tile panorama (c.1700–1725), depicting 14 kilometers of Lisbon's waterfront from the Tagus River perspective. While the view includes some proportional distortion—the Ribeira Palace is deliberately oversized for emphasis—the panorama remains an unparalleled visual record of Lisbon during this era, showing the royal palace, shipyards, churches, and the bustling port that made Portugal master of a global empire spanning four continents.

This reconstruction captures Lisbon at 9:30 AM on All Saints' Day, just ten minutes before the earth would shake for six terrible minutes and change the city—and the world—forever.
